dried (unspecified ingredient)__food.analysis: {"name":"Dried (unspecified ingredient)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"“Dried” describes a processing method and is not an ingredient by itself, so its health impact depends entirely on what has been dried.","details":"Drying is a common food preservation method that removes water to extend shelf life and concentrate flavors and nutrients. Without knowing what is dried (for example, vegetables, meat, fruit), no specific additive- or allergen-related risk can be determined; generally, drying alone does not introduce major health concerns.","category":"Processing descriptor"}

maltose__food.analysis: {"name":"Maltose","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Maltose is a simple sugar that contributes to total sugar intake and calories but is not inherently toxic.","details":"As a disaccharide composed of two glucose units, maltose is digested into glucose and can raise blood sugar levels. High intake of sugars like maltose may contribute to weight gain, dental caries, and metabolic issues, especially for people with insulin resistance or diabetes, but small to moderate amounts are generally well tolerated in healthy individuals.","category":"Sugar / sweetener"}

whey powder__food.analysis: {"name":"Whey powder","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Whey powder is a dairy-derived protein source that is safe for most people but can trigger reactions in those with milk allergy or lactose intolerance.","details":"Whey is the liquid fraction of milk that remains after cheese-making, then dried into a powder rich in proteins and some lactose. It is a common allergen for individuals with cow’s milk allergy and may cause digestive discomfort (bloating, gas, diarrhea) in people with lactose intolerance; for others, it is generally safe and can be a useful protein source.","category":"Allergen (dairy)"}

garlic flake__food.analysis: {"name":"Garlic flake","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Garlic flakes are simply dried pieces of garlic and are generally considered safe and even beneficial for most people.","details":"Garlic contains sulfur compounds that may support cardiovascular health and have mild antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. A small subset of individuals may experience digestive discomfort or have a garlic sensitivity, but for the general population, garlic flakes are a low-risk flavoring ingredient.","category":"Herb / spice"}

paprika color__food.analysis: {"name":"Paprika color","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Paprika color is a natural colorant derived from peppers and is typically low risk as a food color.","details":"This ingredient is usually made by extracting carotenoid pigments (such as capsanthin and capsorubin) from paprika peppers to provide a red to orange hue. Unlike many artificial colorants, paprika color is considered safe for most people, although those with rare allergies to peppers or related plants could theoretically react; it does not commonly contribute to major additive-related health concerns.","category":"Natural colorant"}

enzymes__food.analysis: {"name":"Enzymes","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Enzymes are proteins used in food processing to modify texture, flavor, or shelf life and are generally considered safe for most people.","details":"Food enzymes (such as amylases or proteases) help break down starches, proteins, or fats during processing and are usually present in tiny amounts in the final food. They can sometimes be produced using microbes or fermentation. A small number of people may react if they have specific allergies (e.g., to certain microbial or fungal sources), but this is uncommon and not typically a concern for the general population.","category":"Processing aid / enzyme"}

salt__food.analysis: {"name":"Salt","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Salt (sodium chloride) is essential in small amounts but can be harmful when consumed in excess, mainly due to its sodium content. High intake is linked to elevated blood pressure and increased cardiovascular risk.","details":"Salt provides sodium, an essential mineral involved in fluid balance, nerve function, and muscle contraction. However, many people consume far more sodium than recommended (often via processed foods), which can contribute to high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke, especially in salt-sensitive individuals. Those with hypertension, kidney disease, or heart conditions are usually advised to limit sodium intake and monitor total salt from all dietary sources.","category":"Mineral / Sodium source"}

onion flake__food.analysis: {"name":"Onion Flake","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Onion flake is simply dehydrated onion and is generally safe, offering flavor and some phytonutrients.","details":"Onion flakes are made by drying and sometimes lightly processing onion, concentrating its flavor. They provide the same basic compounds as fresh onion, including sulfur compounds that can have mild antioxidant or anti-inflammatory properties. The main concern is for individuals with an onion or allium sensitivity, who may experience digestive or allergic-type symptoms.","category":"Herb / vegetable seasoning"}

natural flavor__food.analysis: {"name":"Natural Flavor","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Natural flavor is a broad, catch-all term for flavoring substances derived from natural sources; it is generally recognized as safe but lacks transparency.","details":"Under regulations, natural flavors must originate from plant or animal materials, but they can still be highly processed and may include solvents, carriers, or by-products in very small amounts. Because the exact substances are not disclosed, people with certain allergies (e.g., to specific fruits, spices, or animal products) or strict dietary patterns (e.g., vegan, religious dietary rules) may not be able to fully assess suitability. For most consumers, it is not a major safety issue, but the vagueness can be problematic for sensitive individuals.","category":"Flavoring agent"}

onion extract__food.analysis: {"name":"Onion Extract","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Onion extract is a concentrated form of onion used mainly for flavoring and is generally safe for most people.","details":"This ingredient is typically produced by extracting flavor compounds and aromatic oils from onions, sometimes concentrating both taste and aroma. It avoids many of the additives associated with artificial flavors and is similar in health profile to onion itself. As with other onion-derived ingredients, the main concern is for people who have an onion allergy or intolerance, who may react even to small amounts of extract.","category":"Flavoring (plant extract)"}

corn starch__food.analysis: {"name":"Corn starch","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Corn starch is a refined carbohydrate used mainly as a thickener and texturizer and is generally well tolerated for most people.","details":"Corn starch is made from the starchy part of corn kernels and is mostly composed of carbohydrates with little protein, fat, or micronutrients. It is naturally gluten-free, making it suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity, provided there is no cross-contamination. Nutritionally, it offers energy but minimal fiber or vitamins, so the main concern is its contribution to overall refined carbohydrate intake rather than any specific toxicity.","category":"Refined carbohydrate / thickening agent"}

spices__food.analysis: {"name":"Spices","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Spices add flavor and may provide beneficial plant compounds, with low safety concern for most people in typical food amounts.","details":"The term \"spices\" is generic and can include a variety of dried seeds, bark, roots, or fruits (such as pepper, paprika, cumin, etc.), each with its own profile of bioactive compounds. In normal culinary quantities, spices are generally safe and can contribute antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds, though some individuals may be sensitive or allergic to specific spices (e.g., mustard, celery, or certain peppers). The main limitation here is lack of specificity—people with known spice allergies or sensitivities should check for more detailed labeling when possible.","category":"Natural flavoring / seasoning"}

garlic__food.analysis: {"name":"Garlic","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Garlic is a natural seasoning with potential cardiovascular and immune benefits and is safe for most people in food amounts.","details":"Garlic contains sulfur compounds like allicin that have been studied for potential benefits to heart health, blood pressure, and immune function. In typical culinary use, it is considered very safe, though some people may experience digestive discomfort (gas, reflux) or have an allergy or intolerance. Garlic can also mildly thin the blood, so heavy use in supplement form (far above food-level intake) may be a consideration for people on anticoagulant medications, but this is rarely an issue from normal food use.","category":"Natural flavoring / herb & spice"}

whole milk powder__food.analysis: {"name":"Whole milk powder","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Whole milk powder is a dehydrated dairy product that provides protein and fat but is a key allergen and not suitable for those with milk allergy or lactose intolerance.","details":"Whole milk powder is made by removing water from whole cow’s milk, concentrating its proteins (including casein and whey), lactose (milk sugar), and milk fat. It is nutritionally dense and can improve texture and flavor, but it is a major allergen: people with cow’s milk allergy must strictly avoid it, and those with lactose intolerance may experience gas, bloating, or diarrhea, depending on their tolerance level. It also contributes saturated fat and calories, which can matter for individuals managing cholesterol or total energy intake.","category":"Dairy ingredient / allergen"}

palm oil__food.analysis: {"name":"Palm oil","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Palm oil is a common cooking and processed food fat whose health impact depends largely on processing and overall diet pattern.","details":"Palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature and is often used in processed foods for texture and shelf-life. Unhydrogenated palm oil is mostly free of artificial trans fats, but it is relatively high in saturated fat, which can raise LDL (“bad”) cholesterol when consumed in large amounts. The main concerns in processed foods are portion size, frequent use, and, separately from personal health, environmental and ethical issues related to palm oil production.","category":"Refined oil / fat"}

canola oil__food.analysis: {"name":"Canola oil","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Canola oil is a widely used vegetable oil generally considered heart-friendly when used in moderation.","details":"Canola oil is low in saturated fat and contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, including omega‑3 fatty acids, which can support heart health when replacing saturated fats. In processed foods it may be refined and exposed to high heat, which slightly reduces beneficial compounds but does not typically create significant trans fats unless it is partially hydrogenated (which should be listed separately). Overall, for most people it is a relatively low-risk oil within a balanced diet.","category":"Refined oil / fat"}

soy lecithin__food.analysis: {"name":"Soy lecithin","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Soy lecithin is a common emulsifier used in small amounts in many processed foods and is generally considered safe.","details":"Soy lecithin helps blend fats and water, improving texture and shelf stability in foods like chocolate, baked goods, and snack products. It is typically present in very small quantities, and most people tolerate it well, though it is derived from soy and may be of concern for individuals with severe soy allergies or those strictly avoiding soy. It is not the same as whole soy protein and usually contains only trace residual protein.","category":"Emulsifier / additive"}

wheat flour__food.analysis: {"name":"Wheat flour","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Wheat flour is a staple ingredient and a major source of gluten, which is problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.","details":"Refined wheat flour (if not labeled whole) is lower in fiber and some nutrients compared with whole‑grain flour, and frequent high‑intake of refined flours can contribute to blood sugar spikes and lower satiety. It contains gluten, making it unsafe for individuals with celiac disease and potentially problematic for those with non‑celiac gluten sensitivity or wheat allergy. For most people without these conditions, wheat flour is acceptable in moderation, especially when balanced with higher‑fiber, whole‑food choices.","category":"Cereal / gluten-containing grain"}

sugar__food.analysis: {"name":"Sugar","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Sugar adds sweetness and energy but can negatively affect metabolic and dental health when consumed in excess.","details":"High intake of added sugars is linked to weight gain, increased risk of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and cardiovascular disease, as well as tooth decay. Sugar in processed foods often contributes “empty calories” without meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, especially when combined with refined starches and fats. Occasional moderate use is generally fine for most healthy individuals, but frequent or high consumption of added sugars is considered a notable dietary risk factor.","category":"Added sugar / sweetener"}

soy sauce (soybean)__food.analysis: {"name":"Soy sauce (soybean)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Soy sauce made from soybeans is a common seasoning that is high in sodium and a major soy allergen source.","details":"Traditional soy sauce is typically brewed from soybeans, wheat, salt, and water, resulting in a fermented sauce that is very high in sodium, which can contribute to elevated blood pressure and cardiovascular strain when consumed in excess. It is also a significant source of soy allergens and often contains gluten (from wheat), making it unsuitable for people with soy allergy, celiac disease, or gluten sensitivity; some varieties may also include added flavor enhancers like MSG or preservatives, so label checking is important.","category":"Condiment / Allergen / High-sodium ingredient"}

wheat__food.analysis: {"name":"Wheat","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Wheat is a common grain ingredient and a major source of gluten, which is a concern for people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or wheat allergy.","details":"From a general health perspective, wheat itself is not harmful for most people and can be part of a balanced diet, especially in whole-grain form. However, wheat contains gluten and is one of the top food allergens; it can cause serious immune reactions in individuals with celiac disease or wheat allergy and may provoke digestive or systemic symptoms in people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity. Its presence is mainly a risk from an allergen and gluten standpoint rather than from additives, artificial colors, or sweeteners.","category":"Cereal grain; major allergen (gluten)"}

garlic extract__food.analysis: {"name":"Garlic extract","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Garlic extract is a concentrated form of garlic used for flavor and potential health benefits, with minimal additive-related concerns.","details":"Garlic extract typically does not involve problematic food additives, artificial colors, or sweeteners; it is primarily used as a natural flavoring. Most people tolerate garlic well, and it has been associated with potential cardiovascular and antimicrobial benefits, though evidence varies with dose and form. A minority of individuals may experience digestive discomfort or intolerance (e.g., in IBS or FODMAP sensitivity), but this is not a safety issue for the general population.","category":"Natural flavoring"}

tomato powder__food.analysis: {"name":"Tomato powder","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Tomato powder is a dehydrated form of tomatoes used for color and flavor, generally low-risk and largely free from concerning additives.","details":"Tomato powder is essentially concentrated tomato solids and naturally provides color, flavor, and nutrients such as carotenoids (like lycopene). It does not inherently contain artificial colors, flavor enhancers, or preservatives unless such additives are listed separately in the ingredient list. While tomato can be an allergen or trigger reflux or sensitivity in some people, this affects a relatively small group compared to common major allergens like soy or wheat.","category":"Dehydrated vegetable ingredient"}

dried onion__food.analysis: {"name":"Dried onion","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Dried onion is a dehydrated vegetable ingredient used for flavor, with low overall risk and no typical additive-related issues.","details":"Dried onion is usually just onion that has been dehydrated, without added artificial colors, flavors, or preservatives, unless otherwise specified. It contributes natural flavor compounds and some micronutrients in small amounts. Some individuals with IBS or FODMAP sensitivity may experience digestive discomfort from onion, but for most people it is safe and not associated with major health risks related to additives, trans fats, or sweeteners.","category":"Dehydrated vegetable ingredient"}

tomato paste__food.analysis: {"name":"Tomato paste","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Tomato paste is a concentrated form of cooked tomatoes and is generally safe and nutritious for most people.","details":"Tomato paste is typically made from tomatoes that are cooked down and strained, concentrating their natural sugars, acids, vitamins (like vitamin C and A), and antioxidants such as lycopene. It does not inherently contain problematic additives, but individuals with tomato allergies, acid reflux, or sensitivity to acidic foods may experience discomfort. Any concerns about sodium or additives would come from additional ingredients listed on the label rather than the tomato paste itself.","category":"Whole food ingredient"}

fermented milk__food.analysis: {"name":"Fermented milk","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Fermented milk is a dairy product containing live cultures and lactose, generally safe but a concern for people with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.","details":"Fermented milk (similar to yogurt, kefir, or cultured milk) is produced by adding beneficial bacteria to milk, which can improve digestibility for some and may support gut health. However, it still comes from cow’s (or other animal) milk and therefore contains milk proteins (casein, whey) that can trigger allergic reactions and may contain residual lactose that can cause symptoms in lactose-intolerant individuals. People with dairy allergies, lactose intolerance, or strict vegans should consider this a higher-concern ingredient, while it is usually low-risk for the general population.","category":"Dairy / potential allergen"}

citric acid__food.analysis: {"name":"Citric acid","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Citric acid is a common food acidulant and preservative that is generally recognized as safe for most people.","details":"Citric acid is widely used to provide tartness, adjust acidity (pH), and help preserve foods and beverages. Modern citric acid is usually produced by fermenting sugar with certain molds (such as Aspergillus niger), not from citrus fruit directly. While most people tolerate it well, a small number of individuals may experience mouth or skin irritation or report sensitivity, but it is not considered a major allergen or toxic additive at typical food levels.","category":"Acidulant / preservative"}

mono- and diglycerides__food.analysis: {"name":"Mono- and diglycerides","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Mono- and diglycerides are emulsifiers derived from fats that help blend oil and water but can be a source of hidden trans fats.","details":"Mono- and diglycerides are partially broken-down fats used to stabilize texture in processed foods like baked goods, ice cream, and spreads. They are generally recognized as safe, but they can be produced from either vegetable or animal fats and may contain small amounts of trans fats that do not always appear on nutrition labels. For people trying to strictly limit processed fats or avoid potential trans fat intake, frequent consumption of products rich in these emulsifiers may be a concern, though occasional intake is unlikely to pose a major risk for most healthy individuals.","category":"Emulsifier / processed fat source"}

cocoa powder (processed with alkali)__fo.analysis: {"name":"Cocoa powder (processed with alkali)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Cocoa powder processed with alkali (Dutch-processed cocoa) is generally safe, though it is more processed and slightly lower in some antioxidants than natural cocoa.","details":"When cocoa powder is processed with alkali (Dutch processing), its acidity is reduced, resulting in a milder flavor and darker color. This treatment can decrease some of the natural flavonoid antioxidants, but does not typically introduce harmful additives on its own. The main concerns with cocoa products usually come from added sugar, fats, or allergens in the overall food, rather than from the cocoa powder itself; however, individuals sensitive to caffeine or cocoa naturally occurring compounds may still need to limit intake.","category":"Cocoa / flavoring ingredient"}

natural and artificial flavors__food.analysis: {"name":"Natural and artificial flavors","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"A broad mixture of flavoring chemicals; generally recognized as safe but can be problematic for sensitive individuals and those avoiding synthetic additives.","details":"“Natural and artificial flavors” is an umbrella term that can cover dozens of compounds, solvents, and carriers used to create or enhance taste, some of which are synthetic. While they are typically used in very small amounts and are generally recognized as safe by regulators, the lack of transparency makes it difficult to know the exact substances involved, and some people report reactions such as headaches or sensitivities to certain flavor components. For those trying to minimize ultra‑processed ingredients or avoid specific additives (like certain solvents or flavor enhancers), this generic label is a concern because it hides detail.","category":"Flavoring / additive blend"}

honey__food.analysis: {"name":"Honey","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A natural sweetener composed mainly of sugars; safe for most people but still adds significant sugar and calories.","details":"Honey is primarily fructose and glucose, with small amounts of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidant compounds; from a metabolic standpoint it acts largely like other sugars. It is generally safe for healthy adults but can contribute to excess calorie and sugar intake if overconsumed, which is relevant for weight management, blood sugar control, and dental health. Honey must not be given to infants under 1 year old due to the risk of botulism spores.","category":"Natural sweetener"}

dextrin__food.analysis: {"name":"Dextrin","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A processed carbohydrate used as a thickener, carrier, or bulking agent; usually well tolerated but adds refined carbs.","details":"Dextrin is a group of short-chain carbohydrates produced by breaking down starches (often from corn, wheat, or potatoes) and is commonly used to improve texture, act as a carrier for flavors, or provide bulk. In typical food-use amounts it is considered safe, though it contributes refined carbohydrate with little micronutrient value and may raise blood sugar, which can matter for people with diabetes or insulin resistance. Very sensitive individuals with celiac disease may need to verify the source (e.g., wheat-based dextrin), though many products now use gluten-free starch sources.","category":"Refined carbohydrate / texturizer"}

pasteurized milk__food.analysis: {"name":"Pasteurized milk","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"A dairy ingredient that provides protein, fat, and calcium but is a common allergen and contains lactose.","details":"Pasteurized milk has been heat-treated to reduce harmful microorganisms, making it safer for general consumption while retaining most of its nutrients such as protein, calcium, and vitamin B12. However, it is a major allergen; people with cow’s milk allergy must avoid it completely, and those with lactose intolerance may experience digestive symptoms unless they use lactase or choose low-lactose options. For the general population it is nutritionally beneficial, but for individuals with dairy-related conditions it poses a clear risk.","category":"Dairy / common allergen"}

cheese cultures__food.analysis: {"name":"Cheese cultures","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Beneficial bacteria used to ferment milk into cheese; generally safe and may support gut health.","details":"Cheese cultures are specific strains of bacteria (and sometimes molds) added to milk to start fermentation, developing flavor, texture, and acidity in cheese. These cultures are standard in cheesemaking, are not considered harmful additives, and many are similar to or overlap with probiotic species that can have positive effects on gut microbiota. The main concern is indirect: their presence confirms the product is dairy-based, which is relevant for people with milk allergy or severe lactose intolerance.","category":"Fermentation culture / dairy processing aid"}

alkali (e.g. cocoa processed with alkali.analysis: {"name":"Alkali (e.g., cocoa processed with alkali / alkalizing agent)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Alkali in foods generally refers to alkaline agents (like potassium carbonate or sodium carbonate) used to adjust acidity or process ingredients such as cocoa. For most people, typical food-use levels are considered low risk.","details":"Alkalizing agents are common processing aids that modify pH, improve texture, or reduce acidity in products such as cocoa, chocolate drinks, and some sauces. While they can slightly increase sodium or potassium intake depending on the compound used, they are used in small amounts and are approved as safe by major food safety authorities. People on strict low-sodium or kidney-compromised diets may wish to monitor total intake of sodium- or potassium-based additives, but the alkali itself is not associated with major health concerns at normal dietary levels.","category":"processing aid / acidity regulator"}

tomato extract__food.analysis: {"name":"Tomato extract","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Tomato extract is a concentrated form of tomato, supplying natural pigments, flavor, and antioxidants like lycopene. It is generally considered safe and can even offer some nutritional benefits.","details":"This ingredient is usually made by concentrating tomatoes to enhance color, flavor, and beneficial compounds such as lycopene and other carotenoids. It does not typically involve artificial additives by itself, though it may appear in processed foods that contain added salt or other ingredients. The main considerations are for people with tomato allergies or acid reflux, who may need to limit tomato-derived products due to acidity or sensitivity.","category":"natural flavor / concentrate"}

soy protein__food.analysis: {"name":"Soy protein","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Soy protein is a concentrated protein source derived from soybeans and is a common allergen. It is safe for most people, but those with soy allergy or sensitivity must avoid it.","details":"Soy protein (isolate or concentrate) is widely used to boost protein content in processed foods, meat substitutes, and nutritional products. It is not inherently harmful and can support adequate protein intake, but soy is one of the major food allergens, and reactions can be serious in sensitive individuals. Additionally, highly processed soy protein may appear in products that are more refined and may contain other additives, so people aiming to minimize processed foods or with thyroid issues sometimes choose to limit large amounts of isolated soy protein.","category":"protein / major allergen (soy)"}

hydrolysate (likely protein hydrolysate).analysis: {"name":"Hydrolysate (likely protein hydrolysate)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Hydrolysate typically refers to protein that has been enzymatically or chemically broken down into smaller peptides and amino acids. It can improve digestibility and flavor, but may act as a hidden source of free glutamate (similar to MSG) and can be an allergen if derived from milk, soy, or wheat.","details":"Protein hydrolysates are used for texture, improved absorption, and savory flavor enhancement in soups, sauces, snacks, and nutritional products. When proteins are hydrolyzed, they can release free glutamate, contributing to umami taste; in sensitive individuals, this may cause MSG-like reactions, although regulatory agencies generally regard them as safe. The actual risk depends on the source (e.g., milk, soy, wheat) and the consumer’s allergies or sensitivities, but labeling that only says “hydrolysate” without specifying the source is less transparent for people who must avoid particular allergens.","category":"flavor enhancer / protein derivative"}

apple puree__food.analysis: {"name":"Apple puree","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Apple puree is a mashed or finely blended form of apples, usually providing natural sugars, fiber, and flavor. It is generally safe and considered a whole-food ingredient when minimally processed.","details":"This ingredient is commonly used to add natural sweetness, moisture, and fruit flavor to snacks, desserts, and baby foods. Nutritionally, it retains some fiber, vitamins, and phytonutrients found in apples, though very smooth purees may raise blood sugar more quickly than whole apples due to faster digestion. Potential concerns are mainly for people who need to limit fructose or overall carbohydrate intake, or those with specific apple allergies or oral-allergy syndromes.","category":"fruit ingredient / natural sweetener"}

glucose__food.analysis: {"name":"Glucose","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Glucose is a simple sugar used as an energy source and sweetener in many foods. It is generally safe but can be a concern when consumed in excess, especially for people with blood sugar issues.","details":"Glucose is a monosaccharide that raises blood sugar quickly and has a high glycemic index. Regular high intake of added simple sugars like glucose is associated with increased risk of weight gain, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes, particularly when part of an overall high-sugar diet. For healthy individuals in moderate amounts it is considered safe, but people with diabetes or metabolic syndrome need to monitor and limit intake.","category":"Added sugar / simple carbohydrate"}

sucrose fatty acid esters__food.analysis: {"name":"Sucrose Fatty Acid Esters","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Sucrose fatty acid esters are emulsifiers derived from sucrose and fatty acids, used to blend water and oil in foods. Regulatory agencies generally consider them safe at typical use levels.","details":"These compounds (often labeled as sucrose esters of fatty acids, sometimes with E-numbers such as E473) help stabilize textures in processed foods, desserts, and beverages. Toxicological studies have not shown significant safety concerns at approved intake levels, though very high amounts may cause mild digestive effects in some people. They do not contribute majorly to trans fat intake and are considered a low-risk food additive for most consumers.","category":"Emulsifier / food additive"}

dextrose anhydrous (glucose)__food.analysis: {"name":"Dextrose Anhydrous (Glucose)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Dextrose anhydrous is a form of glucose used as a sweetener and quick energy source. Like other simple sugars, it is safe in moderation but can be problematic in excessive amounts.","details":"Dextrose is the D-form of glucose and “anhydrous” means it contains no water; functionally, it behaves as a fast-absorbed simple carbohydrate with a high glycemic index. Frequent or high intake of added dextrose contributes to overall sugar load, which is linked to metabolic issues such as insulin resistance, fatty liver, and dental caries when part of a high-sugar diet. People with diabetes or prediabetes should monitor intake closely, while occasional consumption within total sugar limits is generally acceptable for healthy individuals.","category":"Added sugar / simple carbohydrate"}

banana__food.analysis: {"name":"Banana","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Banana is a whole fruit ingredient that provides natural sugars, fiber, potassium, and other nutrients. It is generally a healthy component of foods for most people.","details":"As a minimally processed fruit, banana offers vitamins (such as vitamin B6), minerals (especially potassium), and soluble fiber that can support digestive and cardiovascular health. The natural sugar content is balanced by fiber and micronutrients, making it very different from isolated added sugars. The main considerations are carbohydrate content for people on strict low-carb or diabetes meal plans, and rare fruit allergies or sensitivities.","category":"Whole fruit / natural ingredient"}

processed honey__food.analysis: {"name":"Processed Honey","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Processed honey is a refined form of honey that primarily acts as an added sugar with some flavor and minimal residual nutrients. Its health impact is similar to other concentrated sweeteners when used in typical processed foods.","details":"Processing (such as heating and filtering) can reduce or destroy some of honey’s natural enzymes and bioactive compounds, leaving it mostly as a blend of simple sugars (fructose and glucose). While it can be considered slightly more complex than pure table sugar, it still contributes significantly to added sugar intake and excess calories, which are linked to weight gain, elevated triglycerides, and increased risk of metabolic disease when overconsumed. It should also be avoided in infants under 1 year due to the risk of botulism, though that risk is more relevant to raw honey than heavily processed varieties.","category":"Added sugar / sweetener"}

skim milk powder__food.analysis: {"name":"Skim Milk Powder","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Skim milk powder is dehydrated low‑fat milk and is generally safe for most people but is a major dairy allergen and contains lactose. It also contributes to overall sodium and sugar (lactose) intake.","details":"Skim milk powder is made by removing most of the water and fat from cow’s milk, concentrating its proteins, lactose, and minerals. It poses a particular risk to people with milk allergy (casein/whey proteins) or lactose intolerance, and is completely unsuitable for those with a strict dairy‑free or vegan diet. For others, it is considered safe in typical food amounts, though it adds some sodium and naturally occurring sugars and can contribute to caloric intake.","category":"Dairy, allergen"}

caramel color__food.analysis: {"name":"Caramel Color","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Caramel color is a widely used brown food color produced by heating sugars; most people tolerate it well, but there are concerns about potential contaminants and its use in highly processed foods.","details":"Caramel color (various classes such as E150a–d) is created by heating sugars, sometimes with ammonia or sulfite compounds, to produce a dark pigment used in colas, sauces, and many processed foods. Certain forms (particularly ammonia-processed types) can contain small amounts of 4‑methylimidazole (4‑MEI), a compound linked to cancer in animal studies, though typical dietary exposures are usually well below regulatory limits. Sensitivity reactions are rare but may occur in sulfite‑sensitive individuals; more broadly, its presence signals a processed product, often alongside high sugar or sodium.","category":"Artificial color / food additive"}

monosodium glutamate__food.analysis: {"name":"Monosodium Glutamate","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is a flavor enhancer that boosts umami taste; authorities consider it safe for the general population, but some individuals report sensitivity and it increases sodium intake.","details":"MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, an amino acid naturally present in many foods, and is widely used to intensify savory flavors in snacks, soups, and ready meals. Large reviews by major health agencies have not confirmed serious health risks at normal intake levels, but a subset of people report transient symptoms (such as headache or flushing) after high doses, especially on an empty stomach. It also adds to total dietary sodium, which can be relevant for people managing high blood pressure or cardiovascular risk, especially when combined with other salty ingredients.","category":"Flavor enhancer (MSG)"}

defatted soybean__food.analysis: {"name":"Defatted Soybean","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Defatted soybean is soy with most of its oil removed, leaving a protein‑rich product; it is nutritious but a common allergen and may come from highly processed or GMO sources.","details":"Defatted soybean is typically produced by extracting soybean oil and using the remaining high‑protein meal for flours, textured soy products, or as a protein source in processed foods. For people with soy allergy, even small amounts can trigger reactions that range from mild to severe. While generally safe and nutritionally beneficial for others, it is often found in highly processed foods and is frequently derived from genetically modified soybeans, which some consumers prefer to avoid, though current safety assessments of approved GMO soy are generally favorable.","category":"Soy, plant protein, allergen"}

yeast extract__food.analysis: {"name":"Yeast extract","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Yeast extract is a natural flavoring rich in glutamates that enhances savory (umami) taste. While generally safe, it can act similarly to MSG and may be an issue for people who are sensitive to glutamates or who need to monitor sodium intake.","details":"Yeast extract is made from broken-down yeast cells and is commonly used in soups, broths, sauces, snacks, and processed foods to boost flavor without labeling MSG directly. It naturally contains free glutamates, which can trigger MSG-like symptoms in susceptible individuals, though this is not common. It may also contribute to overall sodium intake, so people with hypertension or those limiting processed foods may want to watch for frequent or large amounts in their diet.","category":"Flavor enhancer / natural seasoning"}

dried (unspecified dried ingredient)__fo.analysis: {"name":"Dried (unspecified dried ingredient)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"The term \"dried\" alone only indicates that an ingredient has had its moisture removed and does not specify what the actual food or additive is.","details":"Drying is a common food preservation method that reduces water content to extend shelf life and prevent microbial growth. Without knowing what has been dried (e.g., fruit, vegetables, meat, herbs), it is not possible to assess specific allergens, additives, or nutrient impacts, but the drying process itself is generally considered low risk. Any health concern would depend on the underlying ingredient and whether additional additives (like sulfites, salt, sugar, or flavor enhancers) were used during processing.","category":"Processing description / preservation method"}

disodium inosinate__food.analysis: {"name":"Disodium inosinate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Disodium inosinate is a flavor enhancer often used with MSG or disodium guanylate to boost savory (umami) taste. It is generally recognized as safe for most people at typical food-use levels.","details":"Disodium inosinate (E631) is a nucleotide-based flavor enhancer commonly found in snacks, instant noodles, soups, and processed meats. It is usually present in very small amounts, but may indicate a highly processed, strongly flavored product, especially when combined with MSG. Most healthy individuals tolerate it well; however, people who are sensitive to MSG or trying to avoid intense flavor enhancers may prefer to limit it.","category":"Flavor enhancer / food additive"}

modified food starch__food.analysis: {"name":"Modified food starch","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Modified food starch is a processed starch used to thicken or stabilize foods and is generally recognized as safe for most people.","details":"Modified food starch is typically derived from corn, potato, tapioca, or wheat and then chemically or physically altered to improve texture, stability, or resistance to heat and acidity. For most consumers it poses low health risk, but individuals with specific allergies or celiac disease should verify the starch source, because it can sometimes be made from wheat and contain trace gluten unless labeled gluten-free.","category":"Thickener / stabilizer"}

baking (as part of 'baking soda')__food.analysis: {"name":"Baking (as part of 'baking soda')","riskLevel":"low","summary":"The word 'baking' here is not an ingredient itself but part of the name 'baking soda', a leavening agent used in baked goods.","details":"Listed on its own, 'baking' is likely a labeling or formatting issue rather than a separate substance. It should be interpreted together with 'soda' as 'baking soda' (sodium bicarbonate). There is no independent health risk attached to the word 'baking'; the relevant safety assessment concerns baking soda itself.","category":"Labeling / not a distinct ingredient"}

baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)__food.analysis: {"name":"Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Baking soda is a leavening agent used to help baked goods rise and is generally safe when consumed in normal food amounts.","details":"Chemically known as sodium bicarbonate, baking soda reacts with acids in doughs and batters to release carbon dioxide, creating a light, airy texture. While it does add some sodium, the quantity in typical baked products is modest; health concerns mainly arise only with excessive use (such as large supplemental doses), which can disturb electrolyte balance or raise sodium intake significantly.","category":"Leavening agent"}

water__food.analysis: {"name":"Water","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Water is a basic, essential component in foods and is generally safe for all consumers.","details":"Water is used as a primary solvent and base in many beverages and processed foods, contributing to texture, volume, and hydration. It does not add calories, allergens, or additives by itself, so its presence is not a health concern; the overall product healthfulness depends more on the other ingredients that accompany it.","category":"Base ingredient"}

high fructose corn syrup__food.analysis: {"name":"High Fructose Corn Syrup","riskLevel":"high","summary":"High fructose corn syrup (HFCS) is a refined sweetener associated with excess calorie intake and potential metabolic issues when consumed frequently.","details":"HFCS is a liquid sweetener made from corn starch in which some of the glucose has been converted to fructose, resulting in a very sweet, inexpensive sugar source commonly used in soft drinks, candies, and processed foods. High intake of HFCS and other added sugars is linked to weight gain, fatty liver, increased triglycerides, and higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, especially when it displaces more nutrient-dense foods in the diet.","category":"Added sugar / Sweetener"}

corn syrup__food.analysis: {"name":"Corn Syrup","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Corn syrup is a concentrated sugar solution made from corn starch and contributes significant calories with little nutritional value.","details":"Corn syrup is primarily composed of glucose and is widely used to sweeten and improve the texture and shelf life of processed foods and candies. While it does not inherently contain allergens like gluten, high intake of corn syrup and other added sugars can promote weight gain, blood sugar spikes, and dental caries, so regular consumption in large amounts is a health concern even though it is considered safe as a food additive.","category":"Added sugar / Sweetener"}

cocoa__food.analysis: {"name":"Cocoa","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Cocoa is derived from cocoa beans and provides flavor and some beneficial compounds, though it may add a small amount of caffeine.","details":"Cocoa powder contains natural polyphenols and flavonoids that can have antioxidant and potential cardiovascular benefits when consumed as part of a balanced diet, particularly in less-sweetened forms. In typical food products, the main concerns arise more from added sugars and fats than from cocoa itself, although people sensitive to caffeine or with certain migraine triggers may need to monitor their intake of cocoa-containing foods.","category":"Flavoring / Cocoa product"}

reduced iron / ferrous sulfate__food.analysis: {"name":"Reduced iron / Ferrous sulfate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A source of dietary iron added to foods to prevent or correct iron deficiency.","details":"Reduced iron and ferrous sulfate are common iron fortificants used in cereals, flours, and other staple foods to increase iron content and help prevent anemia in the general population. At the levels used in fortified foods, they are considered safe for most healthy people, though excessive supplemental iron can cause gastrointestinal discomfort and is risky for individuals with iron overload conditions (such as hemochromatosis). People already taking iron supplements or with known iron metabolism disorders should monitor total iron intake with a healthcare professional.","category":"Nutrient fortification (mineral)"}

thiamine__food.analysis: {"name":"Thiamine","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Thiamine (vitamin B1) is an essential vitamin commonly added to enriched foods.","details":"Thiamine helps the body convert carbohydrates into energy and supports normal nerve and muscle function. It is routinely added to refined grains that have lost some vitamins during processing, and toxicity from food levels is extremely rare because excess thiamine is excreted.","category":"Fortified nutrient (vitamin)"}

thiamine mononitrate__food.analysis: {"name":"Thiamine mononitrate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A stable, synthetic form of vitamin B1 used in food fortification.","details":"Thiamine mononitrate is widely used to enrich flour and cereal products with vitamin B1, compensating for losses during milling. It is considered safe at typical dietary intakes, with no known serious adverse effects in healthy individuals when consumed at levels used in fortified foods.","category":"Fortified nutrient (vitamin)"}

riboflavin__food.analysis: {"name":"Riboflavin","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is an essential vitamin added to many enriched grain products.","details":"Riboflavin supports energy production, normal vision, and the health of skin and mucous membranes. It is commonly included in enrichment blends for breads and cereals and is regarded as very safe; excess amounts are excreted in urine, which may turn bright yellow but is harmless.","category":"Fortified nutrient (vitamin)"}

folic acid__food.analysis: {"name":"Folic acid","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A synthetic form of folate (vitamin B9) used to fortify foods and support normal cell growth.","details":"Folic acid fortification in grains helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects in developing fetuses and supports red blood cell formation. For most people, intake from fortified foods is safe; however, very high supplemental intakes may mask vitamin B12 deficiency, so people using high-dose supplements should do so under medical guidance.","category":"Fortified nutrient (vitamin)"}

tallow__food.analysis: {"name":"Tallow","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Tallow is rendered animal fat, high in saturated fat and calories, which may affect heart health if eaten in large amounts.","details":"Tallow is typically derived from beef or mutton and is used as a solid cooking fat or ingredient in processed foods. It is rich in saturated fat, which can raise LDL (“bad”) cholesterol when consumed in excess, potentially increasing cardiovascular risk, especially in people with existing heart disease or high cholesterol. On the other hand, it does not usually contain trans fats unless further processed, and small amounts can fit into an otherwise balanced diet.","category":"Animal fat / saturated fat source"}

soybean oil__food.analysis: {"name":"Soybean Oil","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Soybean oil is a common vegetable oil that provides polyunsaturated fats but can be highly processed and may contain small amounts of trans fats if partially hydrogenated.","details":"Non-hydrogenated soybean oil is mostly composed of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats, which can be heart-friendly when used instead of saturated fats. However, in many processed foods it may be refined, deodorized, and sometimes partially hydrogenated, introducing industrial trans fats that are associated with increased cardiovascular risk. It is also a soy-derived ingredient, which can be an allergen for sensitive individuals.","category":"Vegetable oil / potential allergen (soy)"}

contains 2% or less of: glycerin__food.analysis: {"name":"Contains 2% or less of: Glycerin","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Glycerin (glycerol) is a humectant and sweet-tasting compound used in small amounts for texture and moisture, and is generally recognized as safe.","details":"Glycerin is a sugar alcohol–like compound that helps retain moisture and improve mouthfeel in foods, especially in bars, confections, and baked goods. At levels of 2% or less, it contributes modest sweetness and texture without major metabolic effects for most people, though large amounts can sometimes cause digestive discomfort. It is not an artificial color, flavor, or preservative, and it does not contain trans fats.","category":"Humectant / texturizer"}

cocoa processed with alkali (dutch-proce.analysis: {"name":"Cocoa processed with alkali (Dutch-processed cocoa)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Cocoa processed with alkali is cocoa powder treated to reduce acidity and bitterness, which slightly lowers some natural antioxidants but is generally safe.","details":"Also called Dutch-processed cocoa, this ingredient is treated with an alkaline substance to produce a milder flavor and darker color that works well in many chocolate-flavored foods. The alkalization process can reduce certain beneficial flavonoids compared with natural cocoa, so its antioxidant content may be somewhat lower. It is not an artificial additive itself and does not add trans fats, artificial sweeteners, or major allergens, but overall healthiness depends on the sugar and fat content of the final product.","category":"Cocoa / flavor ingredient"}

artificial flavors__food.analysis: {"name":"Artificial flavors","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Artificial flavors are chemically synthesized compounds used to mimic natural tastes and generally considered safe, but they can cause sensitivity in some people and add to overall additive load.","details":"Artificial flavors are complex mixtures of lab-created chemicals designed to reproduce the taste of natural ingredients at low cost and with consistent quality. While most approved flavoring agents have been evaluated for toxicity, the exact compositions are often proprietary, making it hard for consumers to know what they are ingesting. A minority of people report headaches, hyperactivity, or other sensitivity-type reactions to certain artificial flavors, and their presence can be a marker of highly processed foods rather than whole, minimally processed ingredients.","category":"Artificial flavoring"}

titanium dioxide (color)__food.analysis: {"name":"Titanium dioxide (color)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Titanium dioxide is a white colorant used to brighten or whiten foods; while historically allowed in many countries, its safety has been questioned and its use has been restricted or banned in some regions.","details":"Titanium dioxide (often labeled TiO₂ or E171) is an inert mineral pigment used to make foods, candies, and coatings appear bright white or more opaque. Some regulatory bodies, such as in the EU, have moved away from allowing it in foods due to concerns about potential genotoxicity and accumulation of small particles, especially in nanoparticle form, although other authorities still consider it acceptable at current exposure levels. For most healthy adults, occasional small exposures are unlikely to cause noticeable harm, but from a precautionary perspective, frequently consuming products colored with titanium dioxide may not be ideal, particularly for children and people aiming to minimize controversial additives.","category":"Color additive"}

monocalcium phosphate__food.analysis: {"name":"Monocalcium phosphate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Monocalcium phosphate is a leavening agent that helps baked goods rise and is generally recognized as safe when consumed in normal food amounts.","details":"This compound provides a source of acidic phosphate that reacts with baking soda to release carbon dioxide, creating a light texture in baked products. Regulatory bodies consider it safe at typical use levels, and it also contributes a small amount of calcium and phosphate to the diet. Excessive intake of phosphate additives from many processed foods can contribute to high phosphorus load, which may be a concern for people with chronic kidney disease, but monocalcium phosphate alone at normal amounts is not usually problematic.","category":"Leavening agent"}

locust bean gum__food.analysis: {"name":"Locust bean gum","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Locust bean gum is a plant-based thickener and stabilizer derived from carob seeds and is generally well tolerated, though large amounts may cause mild digestive discomfort in sensitive individuals.","details":"Also known as carob bean gum (E410), this polysaccharide is used to improve texture, viscosity, and stability in products like ice cream, sauces, and dairy alternatives. It is not digested in the small intestine and functions as a soluble fiber, which can have mild laxative effects or cause gas and bloating if consumed in large quantities. Allergic reactions are rare, and regulatory agencies generally regard it as a safe food additive within typical usage levels.","category":"Thickener/stabilizer"}

dipotassium phosphate__food.analysis: {"name":"Dipotassium Phosphate","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"A common food additive used as a stabilizer and acidity regulator; generally recognized as safe but can add to overall phosphate and potassium load.","details":"Dipotassium phosphate is often used in processed foods, creamers, and beverages to control pH, improve texture, and enhance stability. In healthy individuals, usual dietary amounts are considered safe, but people with kidney disease or those who must limit potassium or phosphate intake (e.g., some heart or renal patients) should be cautious, as excess intake may stress kidney function and affect mineral balance.","category":"Food additive (stabilizer, acidity regulator)"}

chocolate liquor__food.analysis: {"name":"Chocolate Liquor","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Ground, processed cocoa nibs containing both cocoa solids and cocoa butter; it is the base of dark and milk chocolate.","details":"Chocolate liquor is not alcoholic; the term refers to the thick paste made from roasted, ground cocoa beans. It naturally contains cocoa flavanols (which may have some cardiovascular benefits), cocoa butter (fat), and small amounts of caffeine and theobromine. The health impact depends on dose and overall product composition (sugar, fat), but as an ingredient itself it is generally safe for most people except those sensitive to caffeine or chocolate.","category":"Cocoa/chocolate ingredient"}

defatted soy flour__food.analysis: {"name":"Defatted Soy Flour","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Soy flour with most of the fat removed, rich in protein and used to improve texture and nutrition, but it is a common allergen.","details":"Defatted soy flour is made from soybeans after oil extraction and is high in protein and certain micronutrients. It is widely used in baked goods, meat analogs, and protein-enriched foods. While generally healthful for most people, soy is a major allergen, so this ingredient poses a significant risk to individuals with soy allergy and should be avoided by them.","category":"Soy (legume, protein source, allergen)"}

egg__food.analysis: {"name":"Egg","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Egg is a common whole-food ingredient and a major allergen. It is nutritionally rich but can cause serious allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.","details":"Eggs provide high-quality protein, fats, vitamins, and minerals and are widely used in processed foods for structure, emulsification, and moisture. For people with egg allergy, exposure can lead to symptoms from skin reactions and digestive upset to severe anaphylaxis, so clear labeling and avoidance are critical. Eggs also naturally contain cholesterol, but for most healthy individuals, moderate egg consumption is considered acceptable; however, those with specific medical advice regarding cholesterol should follow their clinician’s guidance.","category":"Allergen (egg)"}

milk__food.analysis: {"name":"Milk","riskLevel":"high","summary":"Milk is a major allergen and common source of lactose; it can cause allergic reactions or intolerance in susceptible individuals.","details":"Milk contains proteins such as casein and whey, which can trigger immune reactions in people with cow’s milk allergy, potentially leading to severe responses like anaphylaxis. It also contains lactose, a sugar that many adults cannot fully digest, causing bloating, gas, and diarrhea in those with lactose intolerance. While nutritionally valuable for those who tolerate it, milk poses a high risk for individuals with milk allergy or significant lactose intolerance.","category":"Dairy (major allergen)"}

sorbic acid and potassium sorbate__food.analysis: {"name":"Sorbic acid and potassium sorbate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Sorbic acid and its salt potassium sorbate are common food preservatives used to inhibit mold, yeast, and some bacteria. They are generally recognized as safe at typical food-use levels.","details":"Sorbic acid and potassium sorbate (E200–E202) are widely used in foods such as baked goods, cheeses, beverages, and sauces to extend shelf life by preventing microbial growth. Most people tolerate these preservatives well; adverse effects are uncommon and usually limited to mild sensitivities or irritation in susceptible individuals. Regulatory authorities, including the FDA and EFSA, consider them safe when used within approved limits, and they do not accumulate in the body because they are metabolized similarly to fatty acids.","category":"Preservative"}

potassium sorbate (to retain freshness)_.analysis: {"name":"Potassium sorbate (to retain freshness)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A preservative used to keep foods fresh by slowing spoilage from molds and yeasts. Considered safe for most people in the amounts used in foods.","details":"Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt of sorbic acid and is one of the most common preservatives in processed foods, wines, and baked products. Safety evaluations have found low toxicity and no strong evidence of carcinogenicity at permitted levels, and it is generally recognized as safe (GRAS). A small number of people may experience mild allergic-type reactions or irritation, but for the general population, health risk at typical intake levels is low.","category":"Preservative"}

agave syrup__food.analysis: {"name":"Agave syrup","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"A sweetener with a low glycemic index but high in fructose. Excessive intake may contribute to metabolic issues similar to other concentrated sugars.","details":"Agave syrup is a concentrated liquid sweetener derived from the agave plant and often promoted as a “natural” alternative to sugar. It typically contains a high proportion of fructose, which, when consumed in large amounts, can burden the liver, potentially contribute to elevated triglycerides, fatty liver, and insulin resistance. In small to moderate amounts it can fit into an overall balanced diet, but frequent or heavy use, especially in processed foods, should be limited much like other added sugars.","category":"Sweetener / Added sugar"}

inulin__food.analysis: {"name":"Inulin","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A type of soluble dietary fiber that can act as a prebiotic. Generally beneficial for gut health but may cause gas or bloating in some people.","details":"Inulin is a fermentable fiber found naturally in plants like chicory root and is often added to foods to increase fiber content and improve texture. It serves as a prebiotic, feeding beneficial gut bacteria and potentially supporting digestive and metabolic health. However, because it is rapidly fermented in the colon, some individuals—especially those with IBS or sensitive digestion—may experience gas, bloating, or discomfort at higher intakes.","category":"Fiber / Prebiotic"}

egg whites__food.analysis: {"name":"Egg whites","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"A high-protein ingredient that is nutritious for most people but a major allergen for some. Can provoke allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.","details":"Egg whites are rich in high-quality protein and commonly used in many food products for structure, foaming, and binding. They are recognized as one of the top food allergens; in allergic individuals, even small amounts can cause reactions ranging from mild hives or gastrointestinal symptoms to severe anaphylaxis. For people without egg allergy, egg whites are generally safe and nutritious, but products containing them must be clearly labeled for allergy risk.","category":"Protein source / Major allergen (egg)"}

xanthan gum__food.analysis: {"name":"Xanthan Gum","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Xanthan gum is a common thickener and stabilizer used in many foods and is generally recognized as safe for most people. Some individuals may experience gas or bloating at higher intakes.","details":"Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide produced by fermentation of sugars by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris and is widely used to improve texture and stabilize emulsions in sauces, dressings, baked goods, and gluten-free products. Regulatory authorities such as the FDA and EFSA consider it safe at typical dietary levels, though large amounts can have a laxative effect or cause digestive discomfort in sensitive individuals. Rarely, people allergic to the source substrate (such as corn or soy used in fermentation) might react, but this is uncommon.","category":"Thickener / Stabilizer"}

agar__food.analysis: {"name":"Agar","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Agar is a gelling agent derived from seaweed and is generally safe and well tolerated. In normal food amounts, it poses little health concern.","details":"Agar (often called agar-agar) is extracted from red algae and used as a vegetarian alternative to gelatin in desserts, jellies, and as a stabilizer in various foods. It is mostly indigestible fiber, which can promote bowel movements and satiety, but in large amounts may cause gas, bloating, or loose stools in some people. Safety authorities regard food-grade agar as safe when used in conventional quantities in foods.","category":"Gelling agent / Thickener"}

cellulose gum__food.analysis: {"name":"Cellulose Gum","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Cellulose gum (carboxymethyl cellulose) is a synthetic form of plant fiber used as a thickener and stabilizer, and is generally recognized as safe. High intakes may cause mild digestive symptoms in some individuals.","details":"Cellulose gum is derived from cellulose (plant cell walls) that has been chemically modified to dissolve in water and create viscosity, improving texture in sauces, ice cream, baked goods, and many processed foods. Regulatory bodies like the FDA and EFSA consider it safe, and it is not known to be carcinogenic or strongly allergenic. Because it behaves as a non-digestible fiber, excessive consumption can lead to gas, bloating, or changes in stool consistency in sensitive people, but typical food levels are unlikely to cause problems.","category":"Thickener / Stabilizer (Emulsifier-type additive)"}

natural__food.analysis: {"name":"Natural","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"\"Natural\" on an ingredient list is vague and not a specific ingredient, and often refers to natural flavors or undefined natural sources. This lack of specificity can hide allergens or processed additives derived from natural materials.","details":"Food labels sometimes use the term \"natural\" as a marketing claim or shorthand for natural flavors or colorants, but regulations allow a wide range of processed substances to be called natural if they originate from plant, animal, or microbial sources. Because it is not a precise ingredient name, consumers cannot easily know what compounds are included, their processing level, or whether they contain allergens such as milk, soy, or nuts. For people with allergies or sensitivities, the vagueness of \"natural\" warrants caution and, if possible, clarification from the manufacturer.","category":"Vague term / Potential flavoring"}

polysorbate 60__food.analysis: {"name":"Polysorbate 60","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Polysorbate 60 is an emulsifier used to keep fats and water mixed in processed foods, and is approved as safe within regulated limits.","details":"It improves texture and stability in products like baked goods, whipped toppings, and some desserts by preventing separation. While regulatory agencies consider it safe at typical intakes, it is a synthetic additive, and some animal data raise questions about very high doses, particularly related to gut barrier and inflammation; these doses are usually far above normal dietary exposure. People aiming to minimize highly processed additives may choose to limit it, but for most consumers occasional intake is not considered a major risk.","category":"Emulsifier / food additive"}

sodium stearoyl__food.analysis: {"name":"Sodium Stearoyl","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Sodium stearoyl (usually part of sodium stearoyl lactylate) is an emulsifying compound that helps improve texture and shelf life of baked and processed foods.","details":"This ingredient is derived from stearic acid (a fatty acid) and is used at low levels to strengthen dough, improve volume, and keep fats and water evenly mixed. It is generally recognized as safe, and typical dietary exposures are low. Sensitive individuals may prefer to limit synthetic emulsifiers overall, but sodium stearoyl itself has not been strongly linked to serious health effects at normal food-use levels.","category":"Emulsifier / dough conditioner"}

lactylate (e.g. sodium stearoyl lactylat.analysis: {"name":"Lactylate (e.g., Sodium Stearoyl Lactylate or Calcium Stearoyl Lactylate)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Lactylates are emulsifiers and dough conditioners widely used in baked goods and processed foods and are generally recognized as safe.","details":"They improve dough strength, crumb structure, and shelf life by helping fats interact better with flour proteins and starches. Lactylates are produced from food-grade fatty acids and lactic acid; they do not contain lactose in amounts that typically affect lactose-intolerant individuals. Usual intake levels are low, and regulatory reviews have not identified major safety issues at approved usage levels.","category":"Emulsifier / dough conditioner"}

cottonseed oil__food.analysis: {"name":"Cottonseed Oil","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Cottonseed oil is a refined vegetable oil often used in processed and fried foods; its health impact depends on its processing and fatty acid profile.","details":"Refined cottonseed oil is high in omega‑6 polyunsaturated fats and, depending on processing, can contain varying levels of saturated and potentially trans fats, especially if partially hydrogenated. The oil must be properly refined to remove natural gossypol, a toxin in raw cottonseed; commercial edible oils are processed to meet safety standards, but the oil still tends to be used in highly processed foods. Frequent consumption of foods rich in cottonseed oil (especially if hydrogenated) can contribute to an imbalanced omega‑6 to omega‑3 ratio and may not be ideal for cardiovascular health compared with oils like olive or canola.","category":"Refined vegetable oil / added fat"}

whey__food.analysis: {"name":"Whey","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Whey is a milk-derived protein commonly used in food products and is a major dairy allergen. It is generally safe for most people but can cause reactions in those with milk allergy or lactose intolerance.","details":"Whey is the liquid part of milk that remains after cheese production and is rich in proteins such as beta-lactoglobulin and alpha-lactalbumin. For individuals with milk allergy, even small amounts can trigger symptoms ranging from hives to anaphylaxis. People with lactose intolerance may also experience digestive discomfort, depending on how much lactose remains in the ingredient and their individual sensitivity. For the general population, whey is considered safe and is widely used in processed foods and protein supplements.","category":"Allergen (dairy protein)"}

corn syrup solids__food.analysis: {"name":"Corn syrup solids","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Corn syrup solids are a dried form of corn syrup used as a sweetener and bulking agent. They contribute added sugars and calories but are generally recognized as safe when consumed in moderation.","details":"Corn syrup solids are produced by dehydrating corn syrup, yielding a powder that is easy to blend into processed foods, infant formulas, and drink mixes. Nutritionally, they are a source of simple carbohydrates that can raise blood sugar and add to overall sugar intake, which, in excess, is associated with weight gain, dental issues, and metabolic problems. They are not the same as high fructose corn syrup, but they still represent added sugar and should be limited as part of a balanced diet, especially for individuals managing blood glucose or metabolic health.","category":"Added sugar / sweetener"}

calcium__food.analysis: {"name":"Calcium","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Calcium is a mineral often added to foods for nutritional fortification. It is generally safe and beneficial at normal dietary levels.","details":"In food products, calcium can appear in various forms (such as calcium carbonate, calcium phosphate, or calcium sulfate) to boost mineral content or improve texture. Adequate calcium intake supports bone health, muscle function, and nerve signaling. Very high supplemental intakes over long periods may contribute to kidney stones or interact with certain medications, but levels in typical fortified foods are considered safe for most people. The specific health and functional properties depend somewhat on the exact calcium compound used.","category":"Mineral / nutrient"}

sulfate__food.analysis: {"name":"Sulfate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Sulfate refers to a family of sulfur-containing compounds sometimes present in food ingredients, often as part of mineral salts. At typical food levels, sulfates are considered safe for most consumers.","details":"In ingredient lists, “sulfate” can be part of compounds like calcium sulfate, magnesium sulfate, or other mineral salts used as firming agents, dough conditioners, or nutrient sources. These sulfates are different from sulfites, which are more commonly associated with allergic-type reactions. Most people tolerate sulfates without issue; very high intakes from non-food sources can cause gastrointestinal upset, but the amounts in foods are generally low and regulated for safety.","category":"Mineral salt / processing aid"}

dextrose__food.analysis: {"name":"Dextrose","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Dextrose is a simple sugar (glucose) used as a sweetener and energy source in many processed foods. It is generally safe but can contribute to blood sugar spikes and excess calorie intake.","details":"Dextrose is a monosaccharide chemically identical to glucose, rapidly absorbed and quickly raising blood sugar and insulin levels. For most healthy people it is safe in moderate amounts, but frequent or high intake can contribute to weight gain, insulin resistance, and poor blood sugar control, especially in people with diabetes or metabolic syndrome. It also adds to the overall ‘added sugar’ load of a product.","category":"Sugar / Sweetener"}

hydrogenated (likely hydrogenated oils o.analysis: {"name":"Hydrogenated (likely hydrogenated oils or fats)","riskLevel":"high","summary":"“Hydrogenated” usually refers to hydrogenated oils or fats, which often contain trans fats that are strongly linked to cardiovascular disease. Even when fully hydrogenated, these fats can still worsen blood lipid profiles when used heavily.","details":"Hydrogenation is a process that adds hydrogen to liquid vegetable oils to make them more solid and shelf-stable, which can create trans fatty acids. Partially hydrogenated oils are a major dietary source of artificial trans fats, which raise LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, lower HDL (“good”) cholesterol, and increase the risk of heart disease and inflammation. Some products use fully hydrogenated oils that contain very low trans fats, but without more context, the presence of “hydrogenated” on an ingredient list is a red flag for unhealthy fat quality.","category":"Fats / Hydrogenated oils"}

sodium acid pyrophosphate__food.analysis: {"name":"Sodium Acid Pyrophosphate","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Sodium acid pyrophosphate is a leavening agent and sequestrant used to control texture and color in processed foods. It is generally recognized as safe but can add to sodium and phosphate intake.","details":"This compound helps baked goods rise and also stabilizes color and texture in processed foods like frozen potatoes or canned products. While approved by food safety authorities, it contributes additional sodium, which can be a concern for people with high blood pressure or those needing to limit salt. It also adds inorganic phosphate, and high overall phosphate intake may be problematic for individuals with kidney disease or certain cardiovascular conditions.","category":"Leavening agent / Additive"}

mono- and diglycerides (mono component)_.analysis: {"name":"Mono- and Diglycerides (mono component)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Mono- and diglycerides are emulsifiers derived from fats that help blend oil and water in processed foods. They are widely used and generally considered safe, but they can add small amounts of trans fats and come from highly refined oils.","details":"Monoglycerides are partial glycerides made from one fatty acid attached to glycerol, used to improve texture, prevent separation, and extend shelf life. They often come from vegetable oils that may be refined, bleached, and deodorized, and can contain trace trans fats even if a product lists ‘0 g trans fat’. For most people occasional intake is not a major concern, but heavy reliance on foods with these additives may reflect a more processed diet with lower overall nutritional quality.","category":"Emulsifier"}

mono- and diglycerides (diglycerides com.analysis: {"name":"Mono- and Diglycerides (diglycerides component)","riskLevel":"moderate","summary":"Diglycerides are the companion to monoglycerides in the common emulsifier pair “mono- and diglycerides,” helping stabilize texture in processed foods. Health concerns are similar: they are generally safe but can be a minor source of trans fats and come from refined fats.","details":"Diglycerides have two fatty acids attached to a glycerol backbone and act as surface-active agents that keep fat and water mixed and improve softness in baked goods, margarine, and many packaged items. They are metabolized as fats and, like monoglycerides, can introduce small amounts of trans fats depending on how they are produced. While regulatory agencies consider them safe at typical use levels, frequent consumption is characteristic of diets high in ultra-processed foods, which are associated with poorer long-term health outcomes.","category":"Emulsifier"}

baking soda__food.analysis: {"name":"Baking Soda","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is a common leavening agent that is generally recognized as safe when used in normal food quantities.","details":"Sodium bicarbonate helps baked goods rise by releasing carbon dioxide when it reacts with acids. The main health consideration is its sodium content: very large or frequent intakes can contribute to excess sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension or kidney issues, but typical amounts in food are small and not problematic for most individuals.","category":"leavening agent"}

lactylate__food.analysis: {"name":"Lactylate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Lactylate usually refers to food emulsifiers such as sodium stearoyl lactylate or calcium stearoyl lactylate, which are widely used and generally recognized as safe.","details":"These compounds are made from lactic acid and fatty acids and help blend water and fat in products like baked goods, margarines, and whipped toppings, improving texture and shelf life. They contain no lactose in meaningful amounts and rarely cause issues; however, extremely sensitive individuals to milk-derived ingredients may prefer to check which specific lactylate is used and whether it is sourced from dairy.","category":"emulsifier"}

potassium sorbate__food.analysis: {"name":"Potassium sorbate","riskLevel":"low","summary":"Potassium sorbate is a preservative added to foods to retain freshness by preventing mold and yeast growth. It is considered safe for most consumers at regulated levels.","details":"Labeled as potassium sorbate (often written as sorbate) and assigned E202 in the EU, this additive helps stabilize products like baked goods, dairy items, and beverages by slowing spoilage. Toxicological studies show a wide safety margin, and global regulators classify it as generally recognized as safe when used as directed. A small number of people may experience mild intolerance or sensitivity reactions, but it is not associated with serious long-term health issues at normal dietary intakes.","category":"Preservative"}

thiamine mononitrate (vitamin b1)__food.analysis: {"name":"Thiamine mononitrate (vitamin B1)","riskLevel":"low","summary":"A synthetic, stable form of vitamin B1 commonly added to enriched and fortified foods.","details":"Thiamine mononitrate is used in many grain products (such as enriched flour and cereals) to replace or boost vitamin B1 levels, supporting normal energy metabolism and nervous system function. It has a long history of safe use in food fortification, and toxicity from thiamine is extremely rare because excess amounts are typically excreted. For the general population, intake from fortified foods is considered safe and beneficial, especially where dietary B1 might otherwise be low.","category":"Nutrient fortification (vitamin)"}
